reply_text:
㊥ (the blank-file trace) I've sent the trace to codex-5. It will run the real Lean v4.29.0 binary on two inputs, an empty file and a file containing only `import Lean`. For each input it records which of the 20,173 initializer-reached declarations are executed, both during initialization and after it. The job is `invoke-1790810292387-29381-d0a50e6b`, parked as `park-552926e7…` with a 90-minute deadline. The packet is in `/tmp/pyreg/packet-envinit-trace.md`.

㊫ (method) Every compiled Lean declaration is a C symbol in the `lean` binary. So the suggested method is to run `lean` under callgrind, which records every function that gets called. The run is split at the point where the frontend starts, and the recorded names are decoded with Lean's own demangler. codex-5 can pick a better method if it gives its reasons.

Some declarations have no symbol, because they were inlined, erased or have no compiled code. Those are counted as "unobservable" and not guessed. There's a check built in: a declaration known to run on an empty file must show up as executed, and a grind propagator must not.

㊟ (what the result will and won't tell us) The result is which declarations actually run on a blank file, split by codex-5's four classes. It also shows whether all 67 parser-table initializers run. It won't cover declarations that are only read as data without being called. Those will fall in the unobservable count, and codex-5 will report that count.

🈝 (callgrind timing) Callgrind makes Lean much slower, so `import Lean` may not finish in time. If it would take more than two hours, codex-5 delivers the empty-file result and says so.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (what I expect it to find) I expect question 2 to matter most. Builtin parsers get into Lean's parser tables only through generated initializers. If those are in the env-init set, part of the 20k is required, not optional.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (how the 20k are used) Native Lean runs all of these at startup. The C code emitted for each module calls its imports' initializers and then its own declarations' initializers (`EmitC.lean:921-943`), so everything in Init, Std and Lean is set up before the frontend begins. So startup "needs" all 20k in the sense that Lean executes them. What we don't yet know is how many of them a blank file then actually reads. That needs a trace, which I propose below. The model can't answer it on its own. Codex-5's write-up is `lean-wiring` `5bf9049`, `census/ENVINIT-USE.md`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (codex-5's split, by what each initializer registers)

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (a mistake in our model) The parser definitions are correctly roots from the grammar side. But the initializers that put them into the parser tables are roots from the env-init side: parser categories, `registerBuiltinParserAttribute` (`Lean/Parser/Extension.lean:519-534`, which I checked), token tables, and so on. Even a blank-file parse depends on those. So the 67 roots / 829 declarations in the parse class belong in the startup set, and the split zai-3 made is wrong for them.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (what the port does) The port doesn't read this census. It pulls source initializers out and runs them, and it has hand-written stand-ins for parser and option initialization (`bootstrap_parser_initialization.py`, `bootstrap_option_registration.py`). Nothing checks those stand-ins against what Lean's initializers actually do. That's the gap in the curriculum on this side.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(what I checked)
- The commit is on the fork.
- The TSV's classes add up to 20,173.
- Two citations match the Lean source: `emitInitFn` and `registerBuiltinParserAttribute`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (next step) I propose a trace in real Lean: run the frontend on an empty file, log which registry and extension entries are looked up, and cross it with this TSV. That would turn "Lean runs 20k" into "a blank file reads N". The upper bound for what startup needs would then be the parse class plus those N. Shall I send it to codex-5?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (kimi-1's alias fix, `2333fab`) The alias table now has all 73 builtin aliases. Each is cited to its registration call in the Lean sources (`Lean/Parser.lean`, `Extra.lean`, `Term.lean`, `Command.lean`, …). An identifier that isn't in the table now raises a named error, where before it was silently treated as an alias. The tests compare three declarations field by field against `#print` output from Lean v4.29.0. I ran them and all 8 pass.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (how "mechanical" the table is) The table is typed out in Python with a citation per entry. It isn't read from Lean when the program runs. That matches how the port records Lean facts elsewhere, but it can fall out of date if the toolchain changes.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (why kimi-1 overran) Most of its three hours went into running each test file before and after its change in `/tmp/mfs-real`. One of those background runs died without starting and had to be relaunched. It's still working on that comparison. So I applied the other fixes in a separate worktree, `/tmp/mfs-pick`, and pushed from there, which leaves the code kimi-1 is measuring untouched. `/tmp/mfs-real` catches up with a fast-forward once kimi-1 finishes.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (reproduction note is incomplete) A fresh worktree also needs `data/tmp/lean/elan/…` (a toolchain copy). Without it, tests fail with `unknown module prefix 'Init'`. The explainer's reproduction steps don't mention this, so they need a line. It's a small fix I'll add at the next docs commit.
